# Question and summarize

# Definition and basics

Let $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a tuple of noncommuting variables,
and let $\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle$ denote the set of all finite words in these
variables, including the empty word $1$.
The free noncommutative polynomial
algebra $\mathbb{C}\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle$ consists of all finite complex
linear combinations of such words.

Equip $\mathbb{C}\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle$ with the involution $\star$ that
conjugates coefficients, fixes each generator pointwise, and reverses words.
Thus $x_i^\star=x_i$ and

$$
(x_{i_1}\cdots x_{i_r})^\star
=x_{i_r}\cdots x_{i_1}.
$$

For $d\in\mathbb{N}$, let $W_d$ be the column vector of all words of length at
most $d$, arranged in a fixed order. A polynomial is a sum of Hermitian squares
(SOHS) if it can be written as a finite sum $\sum_k g_k^\star g_k$. For a
complex vector or matrix, $*$ denotes its conjugate transpose.

:::{#lem-SOS .callout-important icon="false"}
## Gram-matrix characterization of SOHS
Let $f\in\mathbb{C}\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle$ satisfy $\deg f=2d$.
Then $f$ is a SOHS if and only if there exists a Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix
$G\in\mathbb{H}^{|W_d|}_+$ such that $f=W_d^\star G W_d$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

We prove the two implications separately. In the forward implication, the only
subtle point is to show that a SOHS of degree $2d$ can be decomposed using
polynomials of degree at most $d$. For this, we first show that the leading
terms of Hermitian squares cannot cancel.

Let

$$
p=\sum_{k=1}^t q_k^\star q_k\neq 0,
\qquad
D:=\max_{1\leq k\leq t}\deg q_k.
$$

Write $q_k=\sum_u a_{k,u}u$, and choose a word $w$ of length $D$ such that
$a_{k_0,w}\neq0$ for some $k_0$. In the degree-$2D$ part of $p$, the coefficient
of $w^\star w$ is

$$
\sum_{k=1}^t |a_{k,w}|^2>0.
$$

Indeed, a contribution $u^\star v=w^\star w$ of degree $2D$ must have
$|u|=|v|=D$; the unique splitting of words in the free algebra then gives
$u=v=w$. Since every $q_k^\star q_k$ has degree at most $2D$, it follows that

$$
\deg\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^t q_k^\star q_k\right)=2D.
\tag{1}
$$

**Forward implication.** Suppose that $f$ is a SOHS:

$$
f=\sum_{k=1}^t g_k^\star g_k.
$$

If $D:=\max_k\deg g_k$, equation (1) and $\deg f=2d$ imply $D=d$. Hence every
$g_k$ is a linear combination of the words in $W_d$. After fixing the ordering
of $W_d$, there is a unique row vector $c_k\in\mathbb{C}^{1\times |W_d|}$ such
that

$$
g_k=c_kW_d.
$$

Consequently,

$$
g_k^\star g_k = W_d^\star c_k^*c_kW_d,
$$

and therefore

$$
f
=W_d^\star\left(\sum_{k=1}^t c_k^*c_k\right)W_d.
$$

Define

$$
G:=\sum_{k=1}^t c_k^*c_k.
$$

This matrix is Hermitian, and for every $z\in\mathbb{C}^{|W_d|}$,

$$
z^*Gz
=\sum_{k=1}^t(c_kz)^*(c_kz)
=\sum_{k=1}^t|c_kz|^2\geq0.
$$

Thus $G\succeq0$ and $f=W_d^\star G W_d$.

**Reverse implication.** Suppose that $G\in\mathbb{H}^{|W_d|}_+$ and
$f=W_d^\star G W_d$. Since $G$ is Hermitian positive semidefinite, it admits a
factorization

$$
G=C^*C.
$$

For example, if $G=U\Lambda U^*$ is a spectral decomposition, one may take
$C=\Lambda^{1/2}U^*$. Let $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ be the rows of $C$, where
$m=|W_d|$, and define $g_k:=c_kW_d$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
f
&=W_d^\star C^*C W_d \\
&=(CW_d)^\star(CW_d) \\
&=\sum_{k=1}^m g_k^\star g_k.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $f$ is a SOHS, proving the equivalence.

The degree argument above uses the linear independence of distinct words in
the free algebra. It does not carry over unchanged to quotient algebras such as
the Pauli algebra, where relations including $(\sigma_i^a)^2=1$ identify words
of different lengths.

:::

Restricted $\{x_1,\cdots,x_n\}$ to the Pauli operators, i.e., $\sigma_{i}^{I,x/y/z}$ for each site.
A similar Lemma also satisfied, stated as below:

:::{#lem-PauliSOS .callout-important icon="false"}
## Gram-matrix characterization of SOHS
Define the $n$-qubit Pauli string $P_j \in \mathcal{P}_n$ with $4^n$ elements.
A $2^n \times 2^n$ Hermitian matrix $H$ is positive semi-definite iff there exists a $d \in \mathbb{N}$ and correspondingly a vector with $n$-qubit Pauli component $\mathbf{v}:= (P_1,\cdots,P_d)^\dagger$ such that
$$
\begin{align}
H = \mathbf{v}^\dagger G\mathbf{v}, G \succeq 0
\end{align}
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

We prove the two directions separately.

**PSD $\Longrightarrow$ Gram representation.** Suppose that $H\succeq0$. Since
$H$ is a finite-dimensional Hermitian PSD matrix, there exists a matrix $A$
such that

$$
H=A^\dagger A.
$$

The $4^n$ $n$-qubit Pauli strings form a basis of
$\mathbb{C}^{2^n\times2^n}$. Hence, after fixing an ordering of the Pauli
strings, we may write

$$
A=\sum_{j=1}^{d}c_jP_j=\mathbf{c}\mathbf{v},
$$

where one may always take $d=4^n$, and omit zero coefficients if desired.
Therefore,

$$
H
=(\mathbf{c}\mathbf{v})^\dagger(\mathbf{c}\mathbf{v})
=\mathbf{v}^\dagger\mathbf{c}^\dagger\mathbf{c}\mathbf{v}.
$$

Setting $G:=\mathbf{c}^\dagger\mathbf{c}$ gives $G\succeq0$ and
$H=\mathbf{v}^\dagger G\mathbf{v}$.

**Gram representation $\Longrightarrow$ PSD.** Conversely, suppose that

$$
H=\mathbf{v}^\dagger G\mathbf{v},
\qquad
G\succeq0.
$$

Factor $G=C^\dagger C$, and denote the rows of $C$ by
$\mathbf{c}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{c}_r$. Define
$A_k:=\mathbf{c}_k\mathbf{v}$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
H
&=\mathbf{v}^\dagger C^\dagger C\mathbf{v} \\
&=(C\mathbf{v})^\dagger(C\mathbf{v}) \\
&=\sum_{k=1}^{r}A_k^\dagger A_k
\succeq0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $H$ is positive semidefinite if and only if it admits the stated PSD
Gram-matrix representation.
:::

# Moment dual of the Pauli SOHS relaxation

We now derive the moment problem dual to the paper's SOHS relaxation
(Eqs. (3.3) and (3.6), PDF pp. 5--6). Let $W_d$ be the ordered
column of normal-form Pauli strings supported on at most $d$ sites, and let
$[\mathcal P_n]_{2d}:=\operatorname{span} W_{2d}$. Fix $d$ such that
$H\in[\mathcal P_n]_{2d}^{\mathrm{sa}}$, and define

$$
\Phi_d(G):=W_d^\star GW_d.
$$

The degree-$d$ SOHS problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_d:=\max_{\lambda\in\mathbb R,\,G}\quad &\lambda\\
\text{subject to}\quad
&H-\lambda 1\equiv\Phi_d(G),\\
&G\succeq0.
\end{aligned}
$$

## The dual and its relaxation

:::{#thm-PauliMomentDual .callout-important icon="false"}
## Moment dual

For a linear functional $\ell:[\mathcal P_n]_{2d}\to\mathbb C$, set
$[M_d(\ell)]_{v,w}:=\ell(v^\star w)$ for $v,w\in W_d$. The variables
are the moments $\{\ell(u):u\in W_{2d}\}$.
The Lagrange dual of the degree-$d$ SOHS problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_d^\star:=\min_{\ell}\quad &\ell(H)\\
\text{subject to}\quad
&M_d(\ell)\succeq0,\\
&\ell(f^\star)=\overline{\ell(f)},\\
&\ell(1)=1.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

Every density matrix $\rho$ yields a feasible functional
$\ell_\rho(f):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\pi(f))$: its moment matrix is the Gram
matrix of $\{\pi(v)\sqrt\rho:v\in W_d\}$. A truncated feasible
functional need not extend to a density matrix, so the feasible set is larger
than the set of physical states. Therefore,

$$
\lambda_d^\star
\leq\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1}
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\pi(H))
=E_{\mathrm{GS}}.
$$

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

First, for $q=\sum_{v\in W_d}c_vv$,

$$
\ell(q^\star q)=c^*M_d(\ell)c.
$$

Consequently, $M_d(\ell)\succeq0$ is exactly the requirement
$\ell(q^\star q)\geq0$ for every polynomial visible at level $d$.

For weak duality, let $(\lambda,G)$ and $\ell$ be feasible for $(P_d)$ and
$(D_d)$, respectively. Directly from the definitions,

$$
\ell(\Phi_d(G))
=\sum_{v,w}G_{v,w}\ell(v^\star w)
=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(GM_d(\ell)^{\mathsf T}\right).
\tag{2}
$$

Star compatibility makes $M_d(\ell)$ Hermitian. Its transpose is therefore
PSD exactly when $M_d(\ell)$ is PSD. Applying $\ell$ to the primal equality
and using $\ell(1)=1$ gives

$$
\ell(H)-\lambda
=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(GM_d(\ell)^{\mathsf T}\right)
\geq0,
$$

because the trace pairing of two PSD matrices is nonnegative. Thus
$\lambda_d\leq\lambda_d^\star$.

It remains to show that these constraints arise from the Lagrangian. Use
$\ell$ as the multiplier for the equality in $(P_d)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L(\lambda,G;\ell)
&:=\lambda+\ell\!\left(H-\lambda1-\Phi_d(G)\right)\\
&=\ell(H)+\lambda\bigl(1-\ell(1)\bigr)
-\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(GM_d(\ell)^{\mathsf T}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

The supremum over the free scalar $\lambda$ is finite only if
$\ell(1)=1$. The supremum over $G\succeq0$ is finite only if
$M_d(\ell)^{\mathsf T}\succeq0$; otherwise a negative eigenvector $z$ and
$G=tzz^*$ make the Lagrangian diverge as $t\to\infty$. Under these two
conditions the supremum equals $\ell(H)$, which yields $(D_d)$.

Finally, the equality in $(P_d)$ lives in the Pauli quotient algebra, so its
multiplier annihilates the Pauli ideal. In coordinates, this identifies entries
that reduce to the same canonical Pauli string, including their phases. Since
canonical Pauli strings are Hermitian, star compatibility makes their moments
real.
:::

The normalized trace
$\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}(f)=2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(\pi(f))$ gives
$M_d(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}})=I\succ0$. Slater's condition therefore removes the
duality gap, so

$$
\lambda_d=\lambda_d^\star\leq E_{\mathrm{GS}}.
$$

At an attained optimum, equation (2) also gives complementary slackness:
$\operatorname{Tr}(G_{\mathrm{opt}}
M_d(\ell_{\mathrm{opt}})^{\mathsf T})=0$.
